BOOK ENTRY
Salvation — the covenant's enclosure: “thou shalt call thy walls Salvation”; God Himself “a wall of fire round about.” The counterfeit is self-built — wealth's high wall “in his own conceit,” and the whitewashed wall of false peace that the storm flattens.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 60:18; Zech 2:5; Prov 18:11; Ezek 13:10-15) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS

Zechariah 2:5 — For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.
Proverbs 18:11 — The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit.
Ezekiel 13:10 — Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
Ezekiel 13:11 — Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it.
Ezekiel 13:12 — Lo, when the wall is fallen, shall it not be said unto you, Where is the daubing wherewith ye have daubed it?
Ezekiel 13:13 — Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; I will even rend it with a stormy wind in my fury; and there shall be an overflowing shower in mine anger, and great hailstones in my fury to consume it.
Ezekiel 13:14 — So will I break down the wall that ye have daubed with untempered morter, and bring it down to the ground, so that the foundation thereof shall be discovered, and it shall fall, and ye shall be consumed in the midst thereof: and ye shall know that I am the LORD.
Ezekiel 13:15 — Thus will I accomplish my wrath upon the wall, and upon them that have daubed it with untempered morter, and will say unto you, The wall is no more, neither they that daubed it;

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/41x-the-parable-of-the-vineyard.adoc

The week of the cross, in the temple, the chief priests and elders demanded of Jesus by what authority He did these things (Matthew 21:23).
Part of His answer was a vineyard parable Isaiah had already keyed:

Hear another parable: There was a certain householder, which planted a vineyard, and hedged it round about, and digged a winepress in it, and built a tower, and let it out to husbandmen, and went into a far country:

Every man in that courtyard knew the property.
Isaiah had sung it seven centuries earlier — a vineyard planted with the choicest vine, fenced, a tower built in the midst of it, a winepress made therein (Isaiah 5:1-2) — and Isaiah closed his song by handing over the deed:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is decoded by the prophet who planted it.
The remaining symbols are decoded too — the wall, the tower, the winepress, the tenants, and the owner's strange, repeated verb — each one defined elsewhere in Scripture, waiting to be carried in.
Walk the parable with its own vocabulary, and it stops being a fable about ingratitude; it becomes an indictment with every party named, a sentence with a date on it, and the blueprint of the building that rose from the rubble.

Isaiah names the first symbol in the act of removing it.
The song of the vineyard ends with the owner's sentence: “I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down” (Isaiah 5:5).
What a wall is, Scripture states outright — the same prophet, promising Zion restored:

Violence shall no more be heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy borders; but thou shalt call thy walls Salvation, and thy gates Praise.

Isaiah says it twice — “salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isaiah 26:1) — and Zechariah shows the substance behind the masonry: Jerusalem shall be inhabited as towns without walls, “for I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about” (Zechariah 2:4-5).
A wall is salvation — the covenant's enclosure: God Himself around His people, the boundary that divides inside from outside.
Read the vineyard's sentence with the definition installed, and it turns exact: to break down the wall is to withdraw salvation, and what stood inside is trodden down.

Isaiah set the tower “in the midst” of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:2), and the Hebrew Matthew keeps his word — migdal, the same word that stands over Scripture's two defining towers.
Solomon built the first into a proverb: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10) — the Name carrying the Head's Word, covenant law, and fruitful priesthood, sheltering the house that bears it.
Babel raised the second: “let us build us a city and a tower… and let us make us a name” (Genesis 11:4) — the counterfeit, masonry stacked to house a self-made name.
A tower is what a name builds.

The question then answers itself: what stood in the midst of the house of Israel bearing a Name?
God's word to David about his son settles it: “He shall build an house for my name” (2 Samuel 7:13).
The vineyard's tower is the sanctuary — the Name's stronghold planted among the vines.
Redraw the parable's real estate with the labels on: the house of Israel, enclosed in salvation, the temple standing in the middle — let out to tenant farmers, with the owner away and the fruit coming due.

Isaiah's inventory ends on the piece the estate was built to serve.
The owner fenced the vineyard, cleared its stones, planted the choicest vine, raised the tower — “and also hewed out a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2, ASV).
A press is hewn into rock and cannot be moved; the whole property is built around the day its produce is rendered.
Isaiah repeats his verb five verses later — he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and he looked for judgment and righteousness (Isaiah 5:2, 7 — qavah both times) — and the repetition names the crop: the grapes this press was hewed to catch are the fruit by which a nation is judged, its works.

The crop takes one step more: when God comes looking for grapes, what He finds — or misses — is men.
“I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness” (Hosea 9:10); and when Micah walks the stripped vineyard — “there is no cluster to eat” — he names the loss in the next breath: “the good man is perished out of the earth” — and the men who remain “all lie in wait for blood” (Micah 7:1-2).
The blessing side holds the same identification: “As the new wine is found in the cluster, and one saith, Destroy it not; for a blessing is in it: so will I do for my servants' sakes” (Isaiah 65:8) — the remnant spared as good grapes left on the vine.
The works ripen into the people who bear them; the vineyard's yield is persons — which is why what runs from this press, when the vintage is wild, is blood.

Scripture keeps the press's ledger on both sides, and Solomon writes the credit column:

Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.

The bursting press is the blessing itself — Joel promises the same overflow, “the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil” (Joel 2:24) — and the tithe is “reckoned… as the fulness of the winepress” (Numbers 18:27), for the press is where a year's increase is counted and rendered.
Judah's own blessing wears it: “he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes” (Genesis 49:11).
Treading even had its own cry, the heydad, the vintage-shout — grapes trodden and merriment made (Judges 9:27) — and when God sentences Moab, the sentence is a silenced press: “the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease” (Isaiah 16:10).

Joel wrote the overflow clause twice, and the second time the vat holds something else.

Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.

Same vat, same rare verb — overflowing with wine and oil in one chapter, overflowing “for their wickedness is great” in the next.
One press, two vintages: what the vineyard bears decides what runs out of it.
The vintage-shout changes sides the same way — “he shall give a shout, as they that tread the grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jeremiah 25:30) — and the same chapter had already poured the result: “Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations… to drink it” (Jeremiah 25:15).
What the press treads out, the cup serves.

Isaiah's sentence had already routed the vineyard into its own press — the wall broken down, “and it shall be trodden down” (Isaiah 5:5) — and Lamentations records the execution: “the Lord hath trodden the virgin, the daughter of Judah, as in a winepress” (Lamentations 1:15).
The growers went in as the vintage.
Isaiah saw the Treader coming back from that work, and staged the scene as a watchman's challenge and its answer:

Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat?
I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I will tread them in mine anger, and trample them in my fury; and their blood shall be sprinkled upon my garments, and I will stain all my raiment.

Genesis dressed Judah in garments washed in the blood of grapes; the Treader wears the same wardrobe with the other vintage in it, and the stain reads the verdict.
John saw the last run of the press, at full scale:

…Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.
And the angel thrust in his sickle into the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God.
And the winepress was trodden without the city, and blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles…

Isaiah's vineyard was one nation; the last vintage gathers the vine of the whole earth, held until its grapes are “fully ripe” — Joel's press, full because the wickedness is great.
The Rider of Revelation 19 arrives already dressed for it, “clothed with a vesture dipped in blood,” and “he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God” (Revelation 19:13, 15) — Bozrah's Treader, riding out to finish the treading.
The press completes the estate the way it completes the song: the Owner will have His vineyard's yield either way — wine from good grapes, blood from wild.
Everything that happens next in the parable happens because the fruit fell due.

The plot moves on one drumbeat verb.
“He sent his servants… again, he sent other servants… last of all he sent unto them his son” (Matthew 21:34-37) — apostellō every time, the sending that makes an apostle.
Scripture turns that verb into a place in Jerusalem, and interprets the name on the spot:

Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.

Siloam — Isaiah's Shiloah — is the city's gentle spring-channel, and its name is the parable's verb.
Isaiah had already ruled on the cost of refusing it: “Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly… now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 8:6-7).
A flood is an army; refuse the soft Sent water, and the violent water comes.

Jesus filed the same case, with a tower in it.
Told of Galileans slaughtered by Pilate, He answered with Jerusalem's own dead:

Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?
I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.

The tower of Sent fell on men of Jerusalem, and He said “except ye repent” twice (Luke 13:3, 5).
The same chapter holds the name's two poles side by side: eighteen men crushed under the tower, and a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound “lo, these eighteen years,” loosed (Luke 13:11, 16).
Wash in Sent and come seeing; refuse Sent and die under its stones.

Last of all the owner sent his Son — and the tenants “caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him” (Matthew 21:39), which is where history put the cross: He “suffered without the gate” (Hebrews 13:12), outside the enclosure His own parable had drawn.
One Greek word carries the location through both texts and a third — exō, outside: cast out of the vineyard, suffering without the gate, and the winepress “trodden without the city” (Revelation 14:20) — the blood runs outside the wall, every time.
Within the generation the “likewise” was paid in full: “thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee… and shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation” (Luke 19:43-44).
AD 70 executed Isaiah's sentence clause by clause — the wall broken down, the tower in the midst brought down on the city's men, and the vineyard's own participle pronounced over the ruin: “Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles” (Luke 21:24) — Luke's verb is pateō, the treading of the winepress of wrath (Revelation 14:20; 19:15).

The hearers pronounced the verdict themselves — “He will miserably destroy those wicked men” (Matthew 21:41) — and Jesus turned from the story to a psalm, and the turn names the tenants' trade:

Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner: this is the Lord's doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes?

The husbandmen of the story stand as the builders of the psalm — He swapped the words in one breath, and the men in front of Him accepted delivery: “when the chief priests and Pharisees had heard his parables, they perceived that he spake of them” (Matthew 21:45).
The identification is ratified by the accused.

Builders of what?
Scripture keeps a file on the structures Israel's leaders raised while refusing the tried stone.
Solomon set the first structure beside the Name-tower itself, one verse later: “The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit” (Proverbs 18:11) — and the two verses share their Hebrew verb, for the righteous man is set safely on high (sagab) in the Name, while the rich man is high (sagab) only in his own imagination.
Ezekiel watched the trade at work: prophets “saying, Peace; and there was no peace,” building a wall and daubing it “with untempered morter” — and God announcing its inspection: “there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it” (Ezekiel 13:10-11).

Isaiah heard the builders state their charter outright, and recorded the Owner's answer — a foundation and a surveyor's line:

Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death… for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation…
Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.

Amos saw the instrument in the Owner's hand: “the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand… Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel” (Amos 7:7-8).
One Hebrew verb of overflowing — shataph — carries the same flood through every counterfeit in the file: the river over its banks when Shiloah is refused (Isaiah 8:8), the waters over the refuge of lies (Isaiah 28:17), the shower that breaks the whitewashed wall (Ezekiel 13:13).
Every structure the builders raised falls to one water.
They rejected the tried stone because it did not fit the building they had underway — a high wall of conceit, whitewashed, chartered by a covenant with death — and the plumbline that hung against their wall read the verdict the storm executed.

Matthew's word for the vineyard's hedge is phragmos — and the Hebrew Matthew fences the vineyard with gadar, the very root of the wall Isaiah's sentence breaks down.
Paul reaches for the identical Greek word to name one more wall:

For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;

The partition — the phragmos — stood between the citizen and the stranger, “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise” (Ephesians 2:12).
The vineyard's enclosure came down twice, and the two demolitions face opposite directions.
In judgment the wall was removed so that the vineyard could be trodden down (Isaiah 5:5); in mercy the partition was dissolved so that the stranger could come in: “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).
Salvation's boundary was not abolished; it was opened, and the opening runs one way — inward.

The rejected stone went straight to work.
Peter, writing to the scattered, lays the courses:

To whom coming, as unto a living stone, disallowed indeed of men, but chosen of God, and precious,
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood…

Two verses later he sets this chapter's two quarry-texts side by side: “Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious” (1 Peter 2:6, from Isaiah 28:16), and “the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner” (1 Peter 2:7, from Psalm 118:22).
Paul draws the same elevation in the very paragraph where the partition falls: “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple” (Ephesians 2:20-21).
The tower in the midst of the vineyard was a house for the Name built of quarried rock; the house now rising is built of people — every stone alive, set on the stone the builders threw away.

The blueprint's last page still shows a wall.
John measures the city that comes down from God:

And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates… and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel…
And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

The wall, like the tower, is built of names — the tribes on the gates, the apostles, the sent ones, in the foundations — and Isaiah's definition was written for this city all along: walls called Salvation, gates called Praise (Isaiah 60:18).
One symbol of the parable is still in motion.
“Whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder” (Matthew 21:44) — Daniel watched that stone strike, grind the empires to chaff, and then grow, until it “became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth” (Daniel 2:35): the kingdom.
The kingdom is exactly what the Owner deeded away in the sentence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof” (Matthew 21:43).
Which nation bears the fruit, and by what name Scripture calls it, Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim will prove.
